findings.headline: Pooled property fund investment holds £0.19m unrealised loss; Capital & Investment Risk Reserve recommended to increase by 19%

The outturn report recommends increasing the Capital & Investment Risk Reserve from £0.302m (9% of allocation) to £0.47m (14%). The reserve protects against both investment asset volatility and capital programme risks including interest rate and inflation exposure.
findings.matters: Investment losses and need to strengthen protective reserves signal exposure to asset volatility and indicate capital risks are being actively managed but materialising
findings.figures: Unrealised loss £0.19m on £3.3m pooled fund; reserve increase recommendation £0.168m; reserve rising from £0.302m (9%) to £0.47m (14%)

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.paper_title: Item 9 Outturn Report - Appendix D HIWFRA Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: Future borrowing costs flagged as identified risk within Medium Term Financial Plan as gilt yields remain volatile
findings.detail: The report explicitly identifies 'the path for gilt yields and interest rates over the coming years' as 'an identified risk within the MTFP'. Current borrowing secured at 4.74% is significantly lower than anticipated rates for the £38.9m+ of additional borrowing required in 2027–2028. The authority is already monitoring this actively with treasury advisers Arlingclose.
findings.matters: Rising refinancing costs on forecast £38.9m–£43.9m of additional borrowing will directly reduce affordability and MTFP headroom if rates remain elevated
findings.figures: Current borrowing rate 4.74%; Bank Rate 3.75% (December 2025); gilt yields remain volatile; forecast additional borrowing £38.9m–£43.9m due in 2027–2028
findings.quote: The path for gilt yields and interest rates over the coming years will therefore have an impact on future borrowing costs and is an identified risk within the MTFP and will be closely monitored and managed as part of treasury management planning and activity.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.paper_title: Item 9 Outturn Report - Appendix D HIWFRA Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: Debt interest costs exceeded budget by £180k in 2025/26, signalling higher debt service burden ahead
findings.detail: Debt interest outturn was £1.11m against budget of £0.93m on average debt portfolio of £23.7m, a 19% overspend. This budget variance on a core, predictable cost signals either forecasting error or underestimation of debt service impact. With external debt rising and substantial additional borrowing forecast, debt service costs will materially increase.
findings.matters: Budget overruns on debt service indicate forecasting risk and warn that future debt service projections may be understated
findings.figures: Outturn £1.11m vs budget £0.93m, variance £0.18m (19% over), average debt portfolio £23.7m
findings.quote: The outturn for debt interest paid in 2025/26 was £1.11m on an average debt portfolio of £23.7m, against a budgeted £0.93m.

findings.headline: Liability benchmark forecasts £38.9m–£43.9m requirement for additional external borrowing by 2028, exhausting balance sheet resources
findings.detail: Table 7 projects the authority will require cumulative additional borrowing of £38.9m by 2027 and £43.9m by 2028 to fund capital programme commitments. This coincides with forecast depletion of balance sheet resources from -£37.1m to -£7.7m, leaving minimal financial flexibility. The Capital Financing Requirement rises to £44m by 2028.
findings.matters: The scale of future borrowing need combined with falling reserves directly impacts debt affordability and refinancing risk, particularly if gilt yields remain elevated
findings.figures: Liability benchmark forecasts: £9.7m (31/03/26), £38.9m (31/03/27), £43.9m (31/03/28); CFR forecast £44m by 31/03/28; balance sheet resources falling from -£37.1m to -£7.7m

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.paper_title: Item 9 Outturn Report - Appendix D HIWFRA Treasury Management Outturn Report
findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £13m to £27.4m during 2025/26 as authority locked in rates ahead of further rises
findings.detail: The authority took new PWLB borrowing of £15.587m at weighted average rate of 4.74%, simultaneously reducing internal borrowing by £5.5m. This was an explicit strategy to secure fixed rates before anticipated further increases in gilt yields and Bank Rate. The borrowing funds capital programme expenditure and replaces temporary use of cash reserves.
findings.matters: Lenders must understand the authority's debt trajectory, strategic positioning on interest rates, and whether this borrowing pace signals larger debt expansion ahead
findings.figures: External borrowing £27.4m (up from £14.4m), £13m net increase; £15.587m new borrowing at 4.74% weighted average rate; internal borrowing reduced by £5.5m
findings.quote: This borrowing is secured at a weighted average interest rate of 4.74% across three tranches of borrowing and is affordable within the capital financing budget. The borrowing taken out during 2025/26 helps to mitigate interest rate risks, particularly the spike in interest rates that has been seen as a result of recent global events.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Cost per resident at £45.89 places Service in top three of similar fire and rescue services nationally
findings.detail: The Service maintains one of the lowest per-capita costs compared to the defined similar services group (10 comparable fire and rescue services: Avon, Cumbria, Devon & Somerset, Dorset & Wiltshire, Essex, Humberside, Kent, Lancashire, North Yorkshire, West Sussex). This demonstrates strong cost positioning.
findings.matters: Strong cost efficiency vs peers supports financial sustainability and reduces pressure for future council contribution increases
findings.figures: £45.89 cost per resident; top three lowest in similar services group
findings.quote: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service remains in the top three of our similar services group in terms of the lowest cost per resident (£45.89).

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Income generation at £6.7 million in 2025/26, including £1.6 million from asset rental and renewable energy
findings.detail: The Service generates substantial diversified income including asset rental (station buildings, facilities) and renewable energy installations. This revenue helps offset core funding needs and demonstrates asset monetization capability.
findings.matters: Diversified income streams from rentals and renewables provide financial resilience and reduce dependence on government grant funding
findings.figures: £6.7 million total income; £1.6 million from rental charges and renewable energy
findings.quote: the Service continues to generate high levels of income (£6.7 million in 2025/26), including around £1.6 million from rental charges and renewable energy.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Planned improvement activities reduced for 2026/27 due to prioritization of available resources
findings.detail: Directorate improvement activities are being reduced from 2025/26 to 2026/27 (51 planned activities, down from prior year), explicitly stated as due to 'detailed focus on, and prioritisation of, our available resources'. Of the 51 activities, 28 (55%) are 'must do' and 23 (45%) are 'should do'.
findings.matters: Reduction in planned activities due to resource constraints signals budget pressure and may defer service improvements or maintenance
findings.figures: 51 activities planned for 2026/27 (reduction vs 2025/26); 28 must-do, 23 should-do

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Efficiency savings of £2.1 million delivered in 2025/26 through restructures, redesign, and contract savings
findings.detail: The Service achieved £2.1 million in year efficiency savings through team restructures, organisational design changes, service delivery modifications, and licensing/contract optimisations. This demonstrates active cost management but suggests budget pressures requiring ongoing discipline.
findings.matters: Consistent delivery of efficiency savings is essential to affordability, but at this scale it indicates underlying budget pressure
findings.figures: £2.1 million efficiency savings in 2025/26
findings.quote: has delivered significant in-year efficiency savings (£2.1 million) from areas such as team restructures and organisational design changes, Service Delivery changes, and licensing and contract savings.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: On-call availability weak during daytime (47%), creating operational coverage gaps that may drive whole-time deployment
findings.detail: Day-time on-call availability is substantially constrained at 47%, versus 75% at night. While the Service is performing slightly better than the South-East regional average (44%), it trails the similar services average. The paper acknowledges this requires operational workarounds through detachments and deployment strategy.
findings.matters: Poor daytime on-call availability forces increased reliance on whole-time staff or detachments, increasing staffing costs and complexity
findings.figures: On-call availability 64% annual average; daytime 47%, night-time 75%; South-East regional average 44%
findings.quote: On-call availability remains challenging overall, particularly during the daytime (47%) compared to the night-time (75%). The Service also continues to make use of detachments to ensure the most efficient deployment of our workforce

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Whole-time availability declined to 97%, requiring recruitment of 12 new firefighters to restore resilience
findings.detail: Whole-time availability decreased from the prior year to 97%. The Service is recruiting 12 new firefighters in early 2026 and increasing pre-arranged overtime flexibility to address the shortfall. This indicates active capacity pressure.
findings.matters: Declining availability forces increased overtime spend (higher cost) and requires recruitment investment; persistent shortfalls could degrade response capacity
findings.figures: Whole-time availability 97%; 12 new firefighters recruited in early 2026
findings.quote: Whole-time availability was 97%, a slight decrease compared to the previous financial year. However, the recruitment of 12 new whole-time firefighters in early 2026 should help to strengthen resilience in this area, as should renewed flexibility on our use of pre-arranged overtime.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Sickness absence increased to 13.0 days per person, up from 11.6 days, driven by musculoskeletal issues
findings.detail: Staff sickness rose over 2025/26 with musculoskeletal absence as the primary cause. While still below 2023/24 levels, the trend is upward and the paper notes sickness impacts appliance availability, particularly for short-term absence, creating pressure on overtime and staffing.
findings.matters: Rising sickness absence directly increases staffing costs through overtime and agency cover, and reduces operational resilience
findings.figures: Sickness increased from 11.6 days in 2024/25 to 13.0 days in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Service has seen a slight increase in sickness (from 11.6 in 2024/25 to 13.0 in 2025/26); however, sickness levels are still below that of 2023/24 and 2022/23. The main reason for the overall increase in sickness is musculoskeletal related absence

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Finance department budget overspent by £202k, a 12.4% overspend
findings.detail: The Finance service area was budgeted at £1,634k but spent £1,836k. This 12.4% overspend in the financial management function itself is notable and may indicate increased staffing, IT investment, or audit costs.
findings.matters: An overspend in the Finance department raises questions about the adequacy of budget provisions for financial controls and systems, and may indicate emerging costs in audit, compliance, or IT that could grow.
findings.figures: Finance budget £1,634k, outturn £1,836k, variance £202k

findings.detail: Interest costs reached £1,110k against a budget of £930k. This significant overspend suggests either higher than anticipated borrowing levels or higher interest rates on existing debt than were forecast at budget time.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs directly reduce the cash available for service delivery and indicate higher debt servicing pressure, affecting the council's financial sustainability and borrowing capacity.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Premises costs exceeded budget by £931k, a 10.8% overspend
findings.detail: Premises spending came to £9,571k against a budget of £8,640k, the single largest cost variance in the report. For a Fire and Rescue Service where premises include fire stations and emergency infrastructure, this suggests inflation in property costs, emergency repairs, or increased energy and maintenance expenditure that was not forecast.
findings.matters: Sustained premises cost inflation indicates rising infrastructure maintenance and property costs that reduce the council's budgetary flexibility and increase the cost of service delivery.
findings.figures: Premises budget £8,640k, outturn £9,571k, variance £931k (10.8% overspend)

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Fire authority generating income through property partnerships to offset operating costs
findings.detail: The authority is leasing parts of fire station properties (including an overflow car park at Eastleigh for Electric Vehicle Chargers) and enabling co-location with partners to generate revenue. These income-generating arrangements are explicitly intended to offset operating costs that would otherwise be direct costs to the Authority, supporting the National Framework's public value requirement.
findings.matters: Demonstrates active financial management and cost mitigation—the authority is reducing its funding dependency through asset optimization rather than service cuts, which indicates financial discipline a lender would value.
findings.figures: Specific lease income amounts are in an exempt appendix and not disclosed; license fee increase at Stockbridge: £3,772.42 to £3,933.50 plus service charge £5,584.02 to £5,822.46
findings.quote: The income from sharing premises will contribute to offset operating costs which would otherwise be a direct cost to the Authority.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Investment spending constrained as financial position tightens
findings.detail: The document notes that investment in IT systems, fleet renewal, building improvements, and equipment lifecycle management is at risk. It explicitly states: 'As the financial position becomes increasingly challenging there is a risk that it becomes more difficult to plan for and fund this ongoing investment.' This applies to Windows upgrades, mobile data terminals, PowerApps infrastructure, and fleet vehicle replacement.
findings.matters: Deferred IT and fleet investment creates operational risk: older systems fail more often, vehicles spend more time unavailable for maintenance, and productivity tools cannot be upgraded. This can cascade into service delivery problems.
findings.figures: Asset availability examples: gas monitor maintenance costs reduced after lifecycle replacement; electric vehicle rollout ongoing to reduce fuel costs
findings.quote: As the financial position becomes increasingly challenging there is a risk that it becomes more difficult to plan for and fund this ongoing investment.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Funding settlement declining while inflation and delivery pressures rising
findings.detail: The Authority's Medium Term Financial Plan identifies declining local government finance settlement allocation (£40.16m in 2025/26 declining to £37.25m by 2028/29) while total expenditure grows from inflation and delivery cost pressures. This structural mismatch is the root of the 2027/28+ budget gaps.
findings.matters: A declining central funding stream with rising cost pressures and limited operational savings headroom suggests the service will struggle to remain self-sustaining without service reductions, council tax increases, or external support.
findings.quote: The impact of inflation, delivery pressures and lower funding through the settlement resulted in an ongoing budget gap for 2026/27.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Reserve contributions cut and capital financing deferred to bridge 2026/27 gap
findings.detail: The temporary mitigations for 2026/27 include a reduction in planned revenue contributions to capital reserves, reproﬁling of asset expenditure to extend asset lives, and reduced capital financing budgets pending completion of planned spend. The Authority acknowledges these measures reduce future capital funding availability and increase interest rate risk.
findings.matters: Deferred capital spending and reserve contribution cuts are signs of financial stress. They reduce the service's ability to invest in asset renewal and create future liabilities if interest rates rise or assets need replacement sooner than expected.
findings.figures: Reserves balance at start of 2025/26: £31.8m (approximately 35% of total budget); revenue contributions to reserves now temporarily reduced
findings.quote: The planned reduction in reserves contributions means that less funding is available for future capital expenditure than would otherwise be the case and the reduced capital ﬁnancing budget means greater interest risk.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Budget gap closed through one-off reserve draw; structural deficit returns 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget gap was closed via savings delivery and a one-off draw from the Budget Equalisation Reserve. For 2026/27, despite removing over £3m in savings, the impact of inflation and lower settlement funding created another gap. The Authority has closed 2026/27 through temporary mitigations while the Service develops sustainable solutions. The budget tables project a return of budget gaps of £2,702k in 2027/28 and £2,926k in 2028/29, with zero planned reserve funding to cover them.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the service has a sustainable financial model. Recurring gaps that require temporary fixes or reserve draws are a warning sign about long-term solvency and service resilience.
findings.figures: Budget gap 2025/26: £1,813k from reserves; 2026/27: £130k from reserves; 2027/28 onwards: £2,702k–£2,926k projected gap with no identified funding source
findings.quote: The impact of inflation, delivery pressures and lower funding through the settlement resulted in an ongoing budget gap for 2026/27. This is despite removing savings of over £3 million from the budget as part of the existing efficiency programme.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Capital programme entirely self-funded via reserves and borrowing; £15.6m new PWLB borrowing in 2025/26
findings.detail: The authority receives no capital grants from government. The £11.95m capital spend in 2025/26 was funded by £2.9m from capital reserves, £8.2m from prudential borrowing, and £0.6m from capital receipts. During the year, the authority took on £15.587m of new PWLB borrowing at a weighted average rate of 4.74%, described as financing previous internal borrowing while reserves were higher. With reserves now forecast to fall sharply, future capital spending will be increasingly dependent on continued borrowing at potentially higher rates.
findings.matters: The fire authority has no alternative funding source for capital maintenance (estates, vehicles, ICT). As reserves fall and rates remain elevated, the cost of borrowing will rise relative to income. The refinancing risk on maturing debt (currently forecast at 4.74%) against future rates is material.
findings.figures: Capital spend 2025/26: £11.95m; new borrowing taken: £15.587m; weighted average rate: 4.74%; no capital grant received from government
findings.quote: The Authority receives no capital grant from government and therefore capital expenditure is largely funded by reserves and borrowing. There has been an increase in external borrowing during the year as a result.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Emerging budget pressures not yet reflected: business rates, energy costs, pay awards unresolved
findings.detail: A backdated business rate revaluation created an unanticipated £306k pressure in Q4 2025/26, with an ongoing annual cost of £125k going forward that was not in the approved budget. Energy cost pressures from global events could add c.£0.25m in 2026/27. Critically, pay awards for both grey and green book employees have not yet been agreed at the time this report was written, and the budget assumed only 3% inflation. These pressures will compound the existing £2.7m gap from 2027/28.
findings.matters: The authority is already facing a structural gap and has limited headroom in contingencies. New recurring pressures (business rates, energy, employment costs) will either force further cuts or require additional borrowing, both of which reduce flexibility.
findings.figures: Business rates ongoing pressure: £125k; potential fuel cost pressure 2026/27: c.£0.25m; budget assumption for pay: 3%
findings.quote: During Quarter 4 an additional significant pressure of £306,000 arose with respect to the backdated business rates assessment for one of the buildings within the Authority's estate. This creates an ongoing pressure in future years of about £125,000.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Reserves forecast to fall from £35.3m to around £10m over next two years
findings.detail: Current usable reserves stand at £35.3m, but the authority explicitly forecasts these will fall to around £10m over the next two years. This £25m drawdown is driven by the capital programme (estate and vehicle replacement) and the necessity to refresh ICT and equipment. The Authority's policy is that approximately 78% of reserves are fully earmarked for future planned spend, meaning the reserve base is already committed.
findings.matters: A sharp fall in available reserves from £35m to £10m leaves minimal headroom for unexpected pressures or unplanned borrowing needs. It also indicates that the capital programme is being funded out of one-off reserves rather than from sustainable revenue or grant funding.
findings.figures: Current reserves: £35.3m; forecast in 2 years: around £10m; drawdown: c.£25m
findings.quote: Reserves balances are forecast to fall over the next two years to around £10m, particularly as a result of the Authority's continued investment in capital assets and the necessary refresh in ICT and equipment.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Forecast budget gap of £2.7m from 2027/28 with no identified sustainable solution
findings.detail: The authority's Medium Term Financial Plan shows a budget gap of approximately £2.7m from 2027/28 onwards. Temporary mitigations were approved for 2026/27, but the report makes clear that a sustainable solution is still needed from 2027/28. As of the meeting date, options are still being reviewed and worked on; no solution is yet in place. This gap has upside risk due to inflation and emerging service pressures.
findings.matters: A £2.7m structural gap with no plan represents material uncertainty about the authority's financial viability in 2-3 years. For a lender, this signals either unplanned service reductions, further reserve draws, or borrowing that is not yet reflected in forecasts.
findings.figures: Forecast gap 2027/28: c.£2.7m; risk to upside due to inflation and service pressures
findings.quote: Temporary mitigations were agreed in February to address this for 2026/27 and allow a balanced budget to be set but a sustainable solution is needed from 2027/28 onwards.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit: authority would overspend without drawing from reserves
findings.detail: The authority required £1.734m of savings delivery and £1.813m drawn from the Budget Equalisation Reserve to balance a £3.547m budget gap for 2025/26. Despite achieving an underspend, the underlying structural position remains negative: the authority would have overspent by £0.241m without the reserve draw. This dependency on non-sustainable reserves use reveals a structural mismatch between recurring spending and funding.
findings.matters: An authority that cannot balance recurrently without drawing reserves is depleting its capital and reducing resilience. Lenders need assurance that the path is toward structural balance, not ongoing reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Budget gap: £3.547m; BER draw required: £1.813m; overspend without draw: £0.241m; underspend achieved: £1.572m
findings.quote: This is beneficial because the structural position remains negative and the Authority would have overspent by £0.241m without the draw from the BER.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising from 1.8% to 3.2% of revenue funding over the forecast period as borrowing increases.
findings.detail: Prudential Indicator 5 shows the ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream rising from 1.8% (2025/26 actual) to 3.2% (2028/29 forecast). This reflects both increased borrowing and higher interest rates locked in through 2025/26 borrowing.
findings.matters: A rising debt service ratio indicates declining financial flexibility. More revenue is committed to servicing debt, leaving less for service delivery and creating vulnerability to further rate rises.
findings.figures: Financing costs ratio: 1.8% (2025/26 actual) rising to 3.2% (2028/29 forecast)
findings.quote: Prudential Indicator 5 demonstrates that although the Authority has had to increase borrowing to fund capital expenditure, as no capital grant is provided to fire authorities, the cost of financing is relatively low as a proportion of the Authority's funding. The increase reflects the planned prudential borrowing associated with enhancements to the Authority's estate.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Fuel and pay cost pressures are emerging with limited contingency to absorb them.
findings.detail: The report identifies two unresolved cost pressures: rising fuel costs estimated at c.£0.25m for 2026/27, and unresolved pay awards (not yet agreed at time of writing). The budget allocated only 3% for pay inflation. The report explicitly states: 'there is only limited capacity to absorb pressures' and if contingency is used for inflation 'it reduces the ability to respond to other in-year pressures if they develop'.
findings.matters: Pay awards could exceed 3% given public sector pressures. Combined with fuel inflation, these could quickly consume available contingency, forcing reserve draws or service cuts.
findings.figures: c.£0.25m estimated fuel cost pressure for 2026/27, 3% pay inflation contingency in budget
findings.quote: It is estimated that higher fuel costs alone could create a pressure of c.£0.25m in 2026/27... there is only limited capacity to absorb pressures. The contingency budget is however finite and if it is required to meet inflationary pressures it reduces the ability to respond to other in-year pressures if they develop.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Unbudgeted backdated business rates assessment created £306k pressure in Q4 and an ongoing £125k annual cost not included in the approved budget.
findings.detail: In Quarter 4, an unanticipated business rates reassessment added a £306k one-off cost and created a permanent £125k annual pressure going forward. This was not forecast in the approved budget and represents recurring cost the Authority must now absorb.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted recurring cost increases narrow financial headroom and will worsen the 2027/28 budget position. It signals the Authority's budget forecasting missed material liabilities.
findings.figures: £306,000 pressure in 2025/26, creating £125,000 ongoing annual pressure
findings.quote: During Quarter 4 an additional significant pressure of £306,000 arose with respect to the backdated business rates assessment for one of the buildings within the Authority's estate. This creates an ongoing pressure in future years of about £125,000.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: Reserves forecast to fall to £10m over two years while capital investment continues and no government grants are available.
findings.detail: Current usable reserves stand at £35.3m but are forecast to fall to around £10m over the next two years. Simultaneously, 'the Authority receives no capital grant from government and therefore capital expenditure is largely funded by reserves and borrowing'. As reserves deplete, reliance on borrowing increases.
findings.matters: Reserves are the last defence against unexpected costs. Deliberately running them down to £10m while funding capital through borrowing reduces financial flexibility and increases refinancing risk at a time of volatile rates.
findings.figures: Current reserves £35.3m, forecast to fall to £10m over two years. Approximately 78% of current reserves already committed to existing spend programmes.
findings.quote: Reserves balances are forecast to fall over the next two years to around £10m, particularly as a result of the Authority's continued investment in capital assets and the necessary refresh in ICT and equipment. The Authority receives no capital grant from government and therefore capital expenditure is largely funded by reserves and borrowing.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: The Authority borrowed £15.587m at 4.74% to lock in rates before they rise further, signalling expectation of sustained high interest rates.

The report states this borrowing 'helps to mitigate interest rate risks, particularly the spike in interest rates that has been seen as a result of recent global events'. PWLB rates shown rising sharply since February 2026.
findings.matters: Front-loading borrowing to lock in current rates signals management expects rates to stay elevated. This creates permanent increase in debt servicing costs and suggests management views near-term refinancing risk as acute.
findings.figures: £15.587m new borrowing at 4.74% weighted average. Total debt now £27.4m. Forecast new borrowing: £8m (2026/27), £21.8m (2027/28), £21.3m (2028/29).
findings.quote: New external borrowing was taken on during the year as part of the Authority's approved treasury management strategy... The borrowing taken out during 2025/26 helps to mitigate interest rate risks, particularly the spike in interest rates that has been seen as a result of recent global events.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: A £2.7m budget gap forecast from 2027/28 remains unsolved with only exploratory work underway.
findings.detail: The Authority approved temporary mitigations for 2026/27 to set a balanced budget but 'a sustainable solution is needed from 2027/28 onwards'. A £2.7m forecast gap exists. Work to find solutions is described as 'work in progress' with update promised for October 2026. No solutions have been identified yet.
findings.matters: A financial plan without a realistic path to balance the budget signals deteriorating creditworthiness. Lenders scrutinise whether management has credible options to close known gaps.
findings.figures: £2.7m forecast budget gap from 2027/28
findings.quote: Temporary mitigations were agreed in February to address this for 2026/27 and allow a balanced budget to be set but a sustainable solution is needed from 2027/28 onwards.

findings.committee: Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority
findings.headline: The £1.572m underspend masks an underlying structural deficit that required both £1.734m of savings and £1.813m reserve draw to balance the budget.
findings.detail: Without the planned draw from the Budget Equalisation Reserve, the Authority would have overspent by £0.241m in 2025/26. The Chief Financial Officer states the structural position 'remains negative' and notes there is 'a forecast budget gap in future years'. This indicates the Authority's recurring expenditure exceeds sustainable funding.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can sustain itself without drawing reserves. An organisation that appears balanced only through one-off reserve draws and savings programmes faces structural insolvency risk.
findings.figures: £1.572m underspend, £0.241m structural overspend without reserve draw, £1.813m BER draw used
findings.quote: The outturn position is an underspend of £1.572m against the budget, reducing the impact on reserves in year and therefore helping to support the Authority's ongoing financial resilience. This is beneficial because the structural position remains negative and the Authority would have overspent by £0.241m without the draw from the BER.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Investment balances fell £105m in 2025/26 with further significant depletion forecast
findings.detail: Hampshire's investment portfolio decreased from £410.8m to £305.7m in 2025/26 due to DSG deficit growth and drawdown of the Budget Bridging Reserve. The report explicitly forecasts that reserves will reduce significantly over the forecast period due to capital programme funding and continued revenue budget bridging.
findings.matters: Shrinking reserves eliminate financial flexibility, force reliance on new borrowing to maintain operations, and reduce investment income that has previously offset budget pressures.
findings.figures: Investment balances: £410.8m (March 2025) to £305.7m (March 2026), a decline of £105.1m; further reductions forecast
findings.quote: reserves and balances are due to reduce significantly over the forecast period due to the anticipated funding of the Capital Programme and use of the Budget Bridging Reserve to balance the budget

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Cash flow pressures may force short-term external borrowing in 2026/27
findings.detail: Due to uncertainty in the timing of anticipated government DSG deficit grant funding (expected 2026/27 but specific date unknown), Hampshire may need to secure short-term external borrowing for cash management purposes in the next financial year. The report explicitly states longer-term external borrowing may also be needed to fund the outstanding DSG deficit.
findings.matters: Indicates the council faces near-term liquidity pressure and may lack sufficient liquid resources to bridge funding timing gaps, requiring access to short-term debt markets.
findings.figures: Government DSG grant: up to 90% of accumulated deficit; timing: unknown but 'presumably during 2026/27'; current liquid investments £165.7m
findings.quote: short-term external borrowing may be secured in the short term for cash purposes, and also in the long-term to fund the outstanding deficit.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Forecast shows existing borrowing of £217m will be insufficient if capital programme is fully delivered
findings.detail: The council's liability benchmark forecast (Table 8) projects that existing borrowing will not be adequate to meet capital financing requirements in future years. The benchmark is forecast to rise to £572.4m by March 2027 and £920.8m by March 2028, indicating substantial new borrowing requirements of hundreds of millions of pounds in the near term.
findings.matters: Signals the council will need to issue material new debt over the next two years, creating significant new financial commitments and permanent increases in debt service costs.
findings.figures: Forecast liability benchmark: £572.4m March 2027; £920.8m March 2028; current external borrowing £217m
findings.quote: the Council will need to source external borrowing if it is to meet the full delivery of its capital programme.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Liability benchmark moved from negative to positive, signaling end of the council's internal borrowing strategy
findings.detail: In 2025/26, Hampshire's liability benchmark shifted from negative (council had excess balance sheet resources) to positive (council needs external borrowing). The minimum required borrowing increased from negative £75.2m at March 2025 to positive £22.8m at March 2026. This marks a fundamental reversal in the council's financial position from cash-generative to cash-consuming.
findings.matters: This inflection point shows the council has depleted its cash reserves and moved from financial strength to requiring new external borrowing, materially increasing financial risk.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark: negative £75.2m (March 2025) to positive £22.8m (March 2026); existing borrowing £217m
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the County Council moved from having a negative to a positive liability benchmark.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew by £132.6m to exceed £345m cumulatively
findings.detail: Hampshire's special educational needs funding shortfall increased by £132.6m in 2025/26 and now stands at over £345m cumulatively. Although government is providing grant relief covering up to 90% of the accumulated deficit, the council cannot close the ongoing annual funding gap, meaning the cumulative deficit will continue to grow. This structural deficit directly reduces investment income and increases external borrowing requirements.
findings.matters: This structural, growing funding gap will force increased borrowing and reduce resources available for other services, materially worsening the council's financial position over time.
findings.figures: £132.6m increase in 2025/26; £345m cumulative total; government to cover up to 90% of accumulated deficit as at March 2026
findings.quote: Hampshire's DSG deficit grew by £132.6m in 2025/26 and now stands at over £345m on a cumulative basis.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 7i 2026-06-26 Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 clean draft , item 7.
findings.headline: Blanket spend controls introduced requiring approval for all expenditure above £500 threshold
findings.detail: In response to significant forecast in-year overspend in 2025/26, the council formalised directorate spend control boards in January 2025 requiring approval of all spend in excess of £500 with limited agreed exclusions. These crisis-level controls continued throughout 2025/26.
findings.matters: £500 spend controls indicate severe cash management crisis requiring daily intervention and suggest loss of normal financial governance

These controls continued throughout 2025/26.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 7i 2026-06-26 Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 clean draft , item 7.
findings.headline: Statutory funding settlement shows £42m per annum reduction by year 3 of settlement period
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Local Government Settlement provides a three-year period showing incremental increasing reductions in funding each year, resulting in a per annum reduction of £42m by year 3. This structural funding cut occurs against a backdrop of unsustainable budget position.
findings.matters: Significant structural year-on-year funding cuts mean the council's financial position will materially worsen even if spending is frozen
findings.figures: £42m per annum reduction by year 3 of settlement period

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 7i 2026-06-26 Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 clean draft , item 7.
findings.headline: Council unable to identify sufficient recurring savings to close budget gap despite legal minimum service level exercise
findings.detail: A Legal Minimum Service Level exercise was undertaken to identify savings if the council operated at core purpose and legal minimum service levels. This was reviewed by an independent panel, additional savings were identified, but the overall conclusion was that the council cannot find sufficient recurring savings to bridge the budget gap.
findings.matters: Inability to close the gap even at minimum service levels indicates structural financial failure rather than cyclical pressure or discretionary inefficiency
findings.figures: Not quantified as insufficient

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 7i 2026-06-26 Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 clean draft , item 7.
findings.headline: Government rejected two applications for exceptional financial support and above-referendum council tax increases
findings.detail: The council applied for Exceptional Financial Support to raise council tax by 14.99% in 2025/26, rejected by government. findings.matters: Rejected applications mean no external relief is available and the council must close the entire gap through service cuts or continued reserve depletion
findings.figures: 14.99% CTax increase requested 2025/26 (rejected); 9.99% increase requested 2026/27 (rejected)

However, this application was also rejected by Government.

findings.matters: Accelerating reserve depletion shows deteriorating financial position with limited buffer for emergencies, reducing creditworthiness

findings.paper_title: 7i 2026-06-26 Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 clean draft , item 7.
findings.headline: Chief Financial Officer warns Section 114 notice likely for 2027/28 if Council Tax only rises 4.99%
findings.detail: The CFO's Section 25 statement for 2026/27 explicitly warns that if Council Tax increases only to 4.99%, reserves will not be adequate for 2027/28 onwards, and on the balance of probabilities the CFO would have no choice but to issue a Section 114 notice. This is the formal warning of effective insolvency unless government provides support.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals the council cannot balance its budget and is a critical red flag for any lender considering exposure to this authority

findings.detail: The council identifies that the age of its property portfolio is driving more frequent breakdowns and unplanned works, creating budget pressure beyond planned maintenance programmes. findings.matters: Suggests a growing structural maintenance backlog and unpredictable expenditure requirements that could lead to either increasing pressure on future capital budgets or progressive asset condition deterioration.

findings.detail: The council identifies that elevated oil prices are driving significant inflation in construction materials including roofing felts, insulation, plastics and tarmac. This affects the majority of School Condition Allocation funded work and is visible in recent tender prices, with two roofing schemes already revalued upwards.

findings.headline: Uplands Development Infrastructure programme requires £650k unplanned remedial works due to contractor defects
findings.detail: The UDI scheme has identified defects requiring remedial works following discussions with the appointed contractor. findings.detail: Hampshire is proposing to add £2.52m to its capital programme for essential health and safety works on its Adults' Health & Care estate. The council will fund £1.5m through prudential borrowing and £1.02m from the Capital Payments Reserve. The council acknowledges significant financial pressures are driving this investment to address statutory compliance and high-risk issues.

findings.committee: HIWFRA Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: External Audit Results Report 2024-25 -Appendix A , item 89.
findings.headline: Multiple accounting errors across debtors, creditors and property requiring extensive additional audit procedures to resolve
findings.detail: The auditor identified a substantial volume of errors in multiple areas: debtors, creditors, PPE additions (£0.588m classification error identified), PPE existence (£2.337m adjustment to gross book value and depreciation), expenditure and income. In many cases, error extrapolations initially exceeded materiality thresholds and required additional procedures to bring them below reporting levels. The auditor flagged 'volume and value of identified misstatements' as requiring improvement and noted this would result in additional scale fees.
findings.matters: A high volume of errors across multiple accounting areas suggests control environment weaknesses; while errors caught during audit can be corrected, the pattern raises questions about the reliability of the financial control environment and whether other errors may exist.
findings.figures: £0.588 million PPE classification misstatement; £2.337 million PPE existence adjustment; multiple other areas with errors initially above materiality
findings.quote: In many cases, our original error extrapolations were above our materiality threshold and therefore we were required to perform additional procedures to provide further assurance over the population and therefore the overall extrapolated error to a sufficiently acceptable level.

findings.committee: HIWFRA Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: External Audit Results Report 2024-25 -Appendix A , item 89.
findings.headline: Pension liability of £567.8m, predominantly unfunded firefighters' schemes of £542.7m
findings.detail: The authority faces a significant long-term pension obligation. Firefighters' pension schemes represent £542.7m of the net liability of £567.8m, reflecting the defined benefit nature of firefighters' pensions. This is a structural financial burden that constrains cash flow and borrowing capacity and represents a material claim on future revenues.
findings.matters: Lenders assess net debt and long-term obligations when deciding lending capacity; large unfunded pension liabilities reduce the authority's apparent financial flexibility and represent a call on future budgets that reduces capacity to manage other financial pressures.
findings.figures: Total pension liability £567.808 million; Firefighters' Pensions £542.714 million; Injury Pension Scheme £25.094 million
findings.quote: At 31 March 2025 the net liability totalled £567.808m, which was split across the Authority's Pension Schemes: £542.714 million – Firefighters' Pensions Schemes; £25.094 million – Injury Pension Scheme

findings.committee: HIWFRA Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: External Audit Results Report 2024-25 -Appendix A , item 89.
findings.headline: Finance team stretched across concurrent audits of authority and Hampshire County Council
findings.detail: Several finance team members are simultaneously supporting the Hampshire County Council audit while completing the authority's audit. This dual commitment has caused delays in providing audit evidence and reduced availability to support the authority audit, leading to extended audit procedures and additional fees. The auditor explicitly noted that 'timeliness and quality of evidence supporting key accounting estimates' requires improvement, with delays in receipt of information from external valuers and sample queries.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity directly affects the quality of financial controls, the speed of response to queries, and the authority's ability to manage its own affairs; stretched staff are less likely to identify errors before submission and may prioritise one audit over another.
findings.figures: Multiple finance team members shared between two major audits; delays in queries received only at end of October
findings.quote: As noted, several of the Finance Team members were also assisting with the Hampshire County Council audit and this impacted their availability to the Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Authority audit team.

findings.committee: HIWFRA Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: External Audit Results Report 2024-25 -Appendix A , item 89.
findings.headline: New external valuer produced £2.5m in asset overstatements; management declined to correct most of them
findings.detail: The authority switched to a new external valuer in 2024-25. The auditor's real estate specialists found that the valuer's methodologies produced results significantly outside their supportable ranges on tested assets. Winchester Fire Station was found to be overstated by £0.954m (corrected) and three other tested assets had combined overstatements of £1.023m (not corrected by management). A further error of £0.477m was identified in untested assets (also not corrected) and a judgemental difference of £0.988m identified for land assets (also not corrected) because management assessed these as immaterial.
findings.matters: A pattern of overstatements from one valuer suggests systematic errors in methodology or assumptions that could indicate ongoing mispricing of the authority's asset base; management's unwillingness to correct identified errors, even above audit thresholds, suggests potential issues with financial control or judgment.
findings.figures: £0.954 million (Winchester Fire Station, corrected); £1.023 million (three assets, uncorrected); £0.477 million (further error, uncorrected); £0.988 million (land indexation difference, uncorrected)
findings.quote: In applying the assumptions determined by EYRE to the sample of assets tested by the Audit Team, three of the five assets that were tested also fell outside their expected ranges (all overstatements). The total variance across the three assets was £1.023 million. Management have not adjusted for these differences.

findings.committee: HIWFRA Audit and Governance Committee
findings.paper_title: External Audit Results Report 2024-25 -Appendix A , item 89.
findings.headline: Audit qualified due to £44.8m in unresolved property valuations from 2022/23
findings.detail: The authority has moved from a prior-year disclaimer of opinion to a qualified opinion, but the auditor cannot gain sufficient assurance over £31.7m in revalued property, plant and equipment and £13.1m in cost additions from 2022/23. This means material opening balance sheet items remain unaudited, and the auditor cannot confirm the classification of reserves between useable and unusable categories.
findings.matters: Lenders assess asset values to determine borrowing capacity and financial health; unaudited opening balances reduce confidence in the balance sheet and limit the auditor's ability to verify that the year's financial position is fairly stated.
findings.figures: £31.703 million (revalued PPE from 2022/23); £13.144 million (cost additions from 2022/23); total £44.847 million
findings.quote: As a result of the disclaimers of opinion on the financial statements for the years ended 31 March 2023 and 31 March 2024, we do not have sufficient appropriate audit evidence over: the valuation of land and building property, plant and equipment that were last revalued in the financial year 2022/23, amounting to £31.703 million, and additions of £13.144 million

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: The council proposes a 14.99% council tax increase to trigger a referendum, but acknowledges this is unlikely to succeed.
findings.detail: The CFO is recommending a 14.99% council tax increase to trigger a referendum on 7 May 2026. While this would balance 2026/27 with only a £13.3m reserve draw and leave £129.7m for 2027/28, the council's own budget consultation indicates residents are unlikely to approve this level of increase. If the referendum fails, the council defaults to 4.99% and faces the Section 114 scenario.
findings.matters: The council's financial survival strategy depends entirely on a referendum outcome that its own consultation data suggests is unlikely to succeed, leaving no credible contingency plan if voters reject the increase.
findings.figures: 14.99% would require £13.3m reserve draw for 2026/27; would leave £129.7m BBR for 2027/28; referendum scheduled 7 May 2026; consultation feedback indicates likely rejection
findings.quote: the council consider increasing council tax by 14.99%, which would trigger a referendum, but accepts that a referendum is both costly to undertake, with a likely outcome that the proposed council tax rise is not supported

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: The council has a £354m Dedicated Schools Grant deficit currently off-balance-sheet until March 2028.
findings.detail: Hampshire has accumulated a £354m DSG deficit, primarily for Special Educational Needs high needs provision. This sits off-balance-sheet under a statutory override expiring March 2028. Government has announced 90% may be eligible for the High Needs Stability Grant, but this is conditional on submitting a SEND reform plan with payment not expected until Autumn 2026, and eligibility amounts remain unclear.
findings.matters: When the statutory override expires at end-March 2028, this off-balance-sheet liability may be required to be funded through additional borrowing, creating a significant contingent liability that could exceed the new unitary authorities' debt capacity.
findings.figures: £354m forecast DSG deficit; potentially 90% eligible for grant (approximately £319m); override expires 31 March 2028; payment conditional and expected Autumn 2026
findings.quote: The council's forecast DSG deficit at the end of March 2026 is £354m, and will be primarily related to High Needs, although the 'eligible' sum will need to be agreed with DfE and MHCLG

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: The Independent Panel and External Auditor have both concluded the council's financial position is unsustainable and Section 114 is likely.
findings.detail: The 2025 Independent Panel review found that even operating at legal minimum service levels and pursuing all identified savings, the council cannot achieve a sustainable balanced budget. The External Auditor's 2024/25 Value for Money conclusion similarly states the Section 114 risk is pronounced and options to balance future budgets are increasingly limited, though internal arrangements are not the cause.
findings.matters: Independent expert assessment that the deficit cannot be solved through normal management indicates the problem is structural and lasting, not temporary, making financial recovery without government support or major revenue increases impossible.
findings.figures: £734m in recurring savings already delivered since 2008; structural deficit described as unsustainable; both auditor and panel flagged Section 114 proximity
findings.quote: It is evident given the significant savings already delivered, the statutory requirements for service delivery, ongoing demand pressure and reducing government funding together with a reducing pipeline of savings, there is nothing to suggest that the council will be able to close its structural budget deficit in the medium term

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: Reserves will be depleted to £41.1m, insufficient to cover the 2027/28 budget deficit of £179.7m.
findings.detail: The Budget Bridging Reserve currently holds £143.0m. Balancing the 2026/27 budget at 4.99% council tax requires a draw of £101.9m, leaving only £41.1m. The 2027/28 deficit forecast is £179.7m, meaning there will be a £138.6m shortfall that exceeds all remaining reserves across the council.
findings.matters: Complete reserve depletion eliminates the council's financial buffer to absorb unexpected demand, revenue shortfalls, or service pressures, leaving no flexibility and significantly increasing default risk.
findings.figures: £143m available in BBR; £101.9m draw required for 2026/27; £41.1m remaining; £179.7m 2027/28 deficit; £138.6m unmet shortfall
findings.quote: Overall usable reserves are forecast to reduce to £108.7m by March 2027, with only £41.1m remaining in the Budget Bridging Reserve and £6.8m in unallocated earmarked reserves

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: The government rejected the council's request for council tax flexibility, removing the only gradual solution to the structural deficit.
findings.detail: The CFO formally requested MHCLG permission in December 2025 for a 9.99% council tax increase (5% above referendum limit) for both 2026/27 and 2027/28 to smooth the impact on taxpayers. MHCLG rejected this request on 9 February 2026, stating the council cannot raise council tax above the referendum limit except by triggering a referendum.
findings.matters: This rejection signals that central government will not support this council through financial flexibility mechanisms, leaving only the high-risk referendum path or financial failure, with no phased solution available.
findings.figures: 9.99% flexibility would have provided additional £44.4m in council tax income; rejected 9 February 2026
findings.quote: on the 9 February 2026 MHCLG confirmed in the Local Government Finance settlement that the County Council has not been granted the flexibility to raise council tax by up to an additional 5% above the current referendum limit

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: The CFO will issue a Section 114 notice for 2027/28 if the council tax increase is limited to 4.99%.
findings.detail: The report explicitly sets out two scenarios. With a 4.99% increase, the 2026/27 deficit of £101.9m requires drawing the entire Budget Bridging Reserve, leaving only £41.1m. The 2027/28 deficit is forecast at £179.7m, creating a £138.6m shortfall that cannot be covered. The CFO has formally concluded he would have no choice but to issue a Section 114 notice.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration of financial failure that triggers government intervention, restrictions on financial autonomy, and significantly damages creditworthiness and borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £101.9m deficit 2026/27; £179.7m deficit 2027/28; £41.1m Budget Bridging Reserve remaining; £138.6m uncoverable shortfall in 2027/28
findings.quote: on balance of probability, and in accordance with his statutory obligations, that without additional government support he would have no choice but to issue a Section 114 notice in advance of agreeing the 2027/28 budget

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: Council Tax frozen 2008–2015 created permanently unrecovered £111m annual funding gap
findings.detail: Council Tax was frozen to protect residents during austerity. The government provided grant compensation, but that grant was later rolled into general funding and subsequently cut. This created a £111m annual structural shortfall. The 4.99% referendum cap prevents the council from recovering this lost income, permanently trapping it in structural deficit.
findings.matters: This reveals an unrecoverable historical policy decision that has locked the council into permanent structural disadvantage. There is no mechanism within current policy to recover the ground lost, making the deficit a lasting condition.
findings.figures: £111m recurring annual impact from freeze-era funding loss, 4.99% referendum cap
findings.quote: The impact of the freeze and subsequent loss of grant is estimated to have an impact of £111m recurring in 2025/26, i.e. if the freeze grant had not been taken, and council tax had been increased by the maximum allowable, council tax income for 2025/26 would be £111m higher.

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: External borrowing required in 2026/27 as cash reserves exhausted; High Needs Block DSG deficit persists
findings.detail: The council has historically financed itself through internal borrowing from cash reserves. Depletion of those reserves to balance successive budgets means external borrowing will be necessary in 2026/27, adding interest costs to an already stretched budget. The High Needs Block deficit in the Dedicated Schools Grant creates an additional structural problem.
findings.matters: Forced external borrowing due to inability to fund operations from reserves signals financial distress and creates ongoing debt service costs that further strain future budgets. This adds permanent pressure that is difficult to reverse.
findings.figures: Reserves forecast to be insufficient to support internal borrowing; High Needs grant support announced (90% of deficit from end-2025/26) but timing uncertain
findings.quote: due to the significant reductions in cash balances over the course of the year, driven in part by the significant deficit on the High Needs Block of the Dedicated Schools Grant, and the use of the budget bridging reserve to balance successive budgets, the County Council is likely to need to borrow externally during 2026/27.

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 cuts £10.9m in 2026/27 grant, rising to £42.9m annually by 2028/29
findings.detail: The government's new funding formula reduces Hampshire's grant allocation despite the council already being underfunded. This is the opposite of hoped-for policy relief. By 2028/29, the annual reduction reaches £42.9m — equivalent to the entire recurring deficit for next year.
findings.matters: A reduction in core grant at the point of maximum financial stress indicates the council cannot expect government support to resolve the structural deficit. The problem will worsen before it improves, with no offsetting policy relief in sight.
findings.figures: £10.9m reduction 2026/27, £42.9m annual reduction by 2028/29, phased over three-year transition
findings.quote: For 2026/27 the County Council will receive the lowest levels of funding per head of population of any Shire County

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspending by £13.1m in 2025/26 despite significant budget increases; no solution in sight
findings.detail: Adult and Children's Social Care are the council's largest budget pressures and the biggest financial risks. Despite substantial budget growth and cost-of-living support, Adult Social Care is £13.1m overspent in 2025/26. The CFO notes that Hampshire's residential care market is expensive relative to other areas, meaning the council is trapped into high placement costs. Demand management has not arrested the pressure.
findings.matters: Demand-led services that consistently exceed budget indicate either inadequate pricing of statutory obligations or failed demand management. This signals structural weakness in the council's ability to deliver services affordably and sustainably.
findings.figures: £13.1m Adult Social Care overspend 2025/26, 9.0% and 10.1% annual growth nationally in adult and children's social care spend
findings.quote: Despite significant increases in the older adult's budget for 2025/26 we are still seeing an in-year pressure of over £13.1m including delays in the delivery of savings in the current financial year.

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: Reserves depleted by £227.8m in four years; Budget Bridging Reserve will fall to £41.1m after 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has drawn from reserves every year since 2022/23 to balance budgets. The four-year total is £227.8m. Drawing £101.9m in 2026/27 will leave the Budget Bridging Reserve at just £41.1m, insufficient to bridge the £179.7m 2027/28 deficit or absorb any adverse movements.
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer against shocks and demand volatility. Rapid depletion at this rate signals unsustainable operations and severely diminished capacity to absorb unexpected costs or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: £227.8m total draw 2022/23–2026/27, £69.4m drawn in 2025/26 alone, £101.9m planned draw for 2026/27, BBR forecast £41.1m residue
findings.quote: Since 2022/23 Hampshire has had to draw from reserves to balance the budget each year, with the amount drawn down to balance the annual budget increasing every year. The total draw over the 4 year period is £227.8m in total.

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: Structural recurring deficit of £101.9m for 2026/27 driven by historic funding loss and underfunding
findings.detail: The council faces a permanent structural deficit that cannot be closed through operational management alone. Root causes include a £111m annual loss from the 2008–2015 Council Tax freeze (grant compensation was later cut), and Hampshire now receiving the lowest per-capita government funding of any Shire County. The deficit persists even after £40.8m in new savings.
findings.matters: A structural deficit indicates the council's baseline spending commitments exceed its funding, not a temporary problem. This raises fundamental questions about whether the authority can sustain service delivery without permanent funding change or service cuts.
findings.figures: £101.9m recurring deficit 2026/27, £111m annual impact from freeze-era funding loss, lowest per-capita grant funding of any Shire County
findings.quote: The outcome of the budget setting process is that there is a recurring budget deficit of £101.9m for the 2026/27 financial year, and a forecast budget deficit of £179.7m for 2027/28.

findings.committee: County Council
findings.headline: Section 114 notice likely in 2027/28 at current funding levels, signalling financial distress
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly states that if Council Tax rises only by the 4.99% referendum limit, reserves will be insufficient to balance the 2027/28 budget (£179.7m deficit vs £108.1m available reserves). A Section 114 notice — the statutory declaration that an authority cannot set a balanced budget — would then be inevitable. This is the most serious warning a CFO can issue.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals the council cannot meet its obligations and is in financial difficulty. For lenders, it indicates severe operational distress and creates risk around service continuity and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £179.7m forecast deficit 2027/28, £108.1m useable reserves, £71.6m shortfall
findings.quote: on the balance of probabilities, without additional government support, the CFO would have no choice but to issue a Section 114 notice in advance of the 2027/28 budget.

Additionally, the Council's ledger system has limitations that required auditors to perform a higher than normal degree of manual work on transaction listings before sampling for testing of debtors, creditors, income and expenditure.

findings.detail: Auditors identified several significant misstatements in the 2024/25 accounts: £3.2 million overstatement of Right of Use Assets and Lease Liabilities from IFRS 16 implementation; £5 million overstatement of Property, Plant & Equipment due to incorrect floor areas in valuations; and £5.8 million projected overstatement of Creditors arising from insufficient supporting evidence for sampled items. Management corrected the first two errors; the creditors error remains uncorrected despite representing £5.8 million of liabilities.
findings.matters: Multiple material errors indicate deficiencies in the Council's financial control environment and accounting processes. An uncorrected £5.8 million overstatement of liabilities raises concerns about the accuracy of final reported balances.

This request was denied. The Council continues engagement with MHCLG but has exhausted a primary option for bridging its funding gap, narrowing available solutions.
findings.matters: Rejection of EFS request eliminates a potential funding mechanism and increases the urgency of the Council's budget crisis. It signals government does not view the Council's position as eligible for exceptional intervention, increasing Section 114 risk.

findings.headline: Council cannot achieve sustainable budget balance even at legal minimum service levels; Section 114 notice risk pronounced in medium term
findings.detail: The audit concludes that the Council faces challenges so severe that even operating at legal minimum service levels and pursuing all identified savings would leave insufficient recurring resources to balance the budget sustainably. Without exceptional financial support, a Section 114 notice (formally confirming inability to balance the budget) becomes increasingly likely in the medium term. This represents a critical structural insolvency risk.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice severely constrains council operations and is a major credit event. For lenders, it signals the council may be unable to meet financial obligations and that services could be drastically curtailed or subject to government intervention.
findings.figures: Medium-term Section 114 risk assessed as 'pronounced'; structural deficit persists across multiple future years
findings.quote: It is apparent that even if the Council were to operate at legal minimum service levels and pursue the savings, efficiencies and income generation opportunities it has identified, it is highly unlikely that there will be sufficient recurring resources to balance the budget on a sustainable basis in the medium and longer term.

findings.headline: Third consecutive year of disclaimed audit opinion due to insufficient assurance over opening balances
findings.detail: For 2024-25, the auditors expect to issue a disclaimed opinion, following disclaimers in 2023/24 and 2022/23. Despite continued audit work on closing balances and in-year transactions, the Council lacks assurance over brought-forward balances from prior years where disclaimers were issued. The auditors cannot rebuild this assurance by the 27 February 2026 backstop date, preventing a clean opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the auditors cannot verify the accuracy or completeness of financial statements, creating fundamental uncertainty about the reliability of the Council's reported financial position and limiting reliance on published accounts.
findings.figures: Third consecutive annual disclaimer (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25); backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: As a result of the disclaimer of opinion on the 2023/24 financial statements, we do not have assurance over some brought forward balances from 2023/24 where we did not gain assurance. This means we do not have assurance over all 2024/25 in-year movements and the comparative prior year movements.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Pooled fund investments are currently valued at an unrealised capital loss of £3.6m, with statutory override exempting them from accounts only until 31 March 2028.
findings.detail: The council's strategic pooled fund investments (equities and property) are held at a net unrealised loss of £3.6m as at the report date. A statutory override currently exempts the council from recognising these losses in the accounts, but this exemption expires on 31 March 2028 for investments made before 1 April 2024. After that date, any losses and gains must be reflected in the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement, which will impact reported reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that reported reserves include a £3.6m unrealised loss that will be forced into the accounts within two years, reducing reported financial resilience. This is a ticking accounting cliff that will hit exactly when the council is forecast to be in maximum cash pressure.
findings.figures: £3.6m unrealised capital loss; Exemption expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: At the current time, the County Council's pooled fund investments are valued with an unrealised capital loss of £3.6m. To date, the statutory override in place on IFRS 9 for local authorities exempts the County Council from taking this unrealised loss to the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement (CIES). This override has been extended to 31 March 2028 for investments made before 1 April 2024, at which time the County Council will be expected to reflect any gains and losses in the CIES.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Hampshire has stated publicly since 2018 that without fundamental funding change, it will not be financially sustainable, and the balance sheet forecast 'starkly presents the scale of the challenge'.
findings.detail: The council's own explicit position, stated consistently for eight years, is that current funding arrangements are unsustainable. The treasury strategy notes that the balance sheet forecast 'starkly presents the scale of the challenge facing the Council over the coming years in the absence of such a change' to government funding.
findings.matters: This is the council's own sustainability assessment. A lender is reading an official acknowledgement that the current trajectory is unsustainable without external intervention (government funding reform). This is not optimistic about the council's long-term position under present conditions.
findings.figures: Position stated consistently since 2018
findings.quote: Since 2018 the County Council has publicly and consistently said that without fundamental changes to the way in which local government is funded, it will not be financially sustainable. The balance sheet forecast starkly presents the scale of the challenge facing the Council over the coming years in the absence of such a change.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Section 114 notice risk is explicitly named as a factor in capital financing decisions.
findings.detail: The council is considering using Capital Payments Reserve (CPR) revenue reserves to support the Budget Bridging Reserve, which would require increasing borrowing to compensate. Officers describe this as a way to 'reduce the prospect/delay the timing of potentially having to issue a Section 114 notice' — the statutory mechanism by which a council declares it cannot balance its budget.
findings.matters: Section 114 notices are the most serious financial governance warning for a local authority. The fact that the council is actively considering policy decisions to delay the prospect of one indicates meaningful near-term financial stress beyond normal budget pressures.
findings.figures: Section 114 notice risk mentioned in capital financing strategy
findings.quote: If we need to reduce the level of CPR revenue reserves supporting the capital programme, effectively we would need to increase the Capital Financing Requirement and secure additional borrowing, to then release the CPR revenue reserves to support the council's short term financial position and to reduce the prospect/delay the timing of potentially having to issue a Section 114 notice.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: Council forecast to require £640m of new external borrowing by 2028/29, with external borrowing beginning in 2026/27 if capital and reserves are fully delivered as planned.
findings.detail: The balance sheet forecast (Table 1) shows the council currently holds £156m of treasury borrowing and £324.1m of investments. From 2026/27, the council's existing internal borrowing will no longer be sufficient to meet the liability benchmark, requiring external borrowing. The liability benchmark forecast shows net borrowing requirement of £488.4m in 2026/27, growing to £836.0m in 2028/29. By 2028/29, new external borrowing is forecast at £640m.
findings.matters: A lender assessing Hampshire needs to know the timing and scale of future borrowing requirements. The forecast requirement to nearly double external debt over three years reflects a structural deterioration in cash position driven by statutory commitments and service pressure spending.
findings.figures: Current borrowing £156m; Investment balances £324.1m; 2026/27 net loans requirement £488.4m; 2027/28 £836.0m; 2028/29 new borrowing £640m
findings.quote: Therefore Table 2 and Graph 1 illustrate that from 2026/27 the Council's existing borrowing is forecast to no longer be sufficient to meet the liability benchmark and the Council will need to source external borrowing if it is to meet the full delivery of its capital programme.

findings.committee: Audit Committee
findings.headline: DSG deficit to grow to over £1,062m by 2028/29, forcing external borrowing one year earlier than otherwise needed and eliminating interest income.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will reach £354m cumulatively by March 2026, with an ongoing annual deficit of circa £200m. This statutory override allows the deficit to sit as an unusable reserve on the balance sheet. The forecast DSG deficit reaching over £1,062m by 2028/29 will deplete cash reserves, forcing the council to borrow for capital purposes earlier than capital financing needs alone would require. The council will lose over £14m of interest income in 2025/26 and £18m in 2026/27 as a direct result.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that nearly £1.1bn of the council's balance sheet is non-distributable and locked by statute. This structural deficit is forcing liquidity management into external borrowing earlier than planned, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £354m cumulative by March 2026; £200m annual deficit; £1,062m by end 2028/29; £14m lost interest income 2025/26; £18m lost interest income 2026/27
findings.quote: Reserves and balances are due to reduce significantly over the forecast period due to the anticipated funding of the Capital Programme and use of the Budget Bridging Reserve to balance the budget pending further savings to be planned and delivered, whilst the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit unusable reserve is forecast to continue to grow, reaching over £1,062m by the end of 2028/29.
